content:
Quick answer: Bands are a cheap, joint-friendly way to build strength with arthritis. Choose a light band, use loops or handles if your hands are sore, and do 8 to 12 slow repetitions of 6 to 8 exercises, two or three times a week. Move up a band when 12 repetitions feel easy, and stop if a joint hurts sharply or swells.

Resistance bands are long strips or loops of stretchy material that you pull against to make your muscles work. They are cheap, light, easy to store and gentle on joints, which makes them one of the best tools for strength training with arthritis at home. This guide explains how to choose a band, how to hold and anchor it if your hands are sore, and gives you three simple routines with a 10-week plan to build up safely.

Why bands suit arthritis

  • Smooth resistance. Bands give a steady, controlled load without the jolts that can come with heavy weights.
  • Easy to adjust. You can make an exercise easier or harder by changing the band, your grip or how far you stretch it.
  • Seated or standing. Almost every exercise can be done from a chair.
  • Whole-body strength. The UK Chief Medical Officers recommend muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days a week, working the major muscle groups. Bands make this possible at home.
  • Joint support. NICE guideline NG226 recommends muscle strengthening as part of exercise for osteoarthritis. Stronger muscles support and protect painful joints.

Choosing your band

TypeWhat it isGood for
Flat bandA long flat strip, often around 1.5 to 2 metresMost exercises; can be tied into loops or wrapped around feet
Tube band with handlesA rubber tube with foam or plastic handlesPeople who find gripping a flat band hard; upper-body exercises
Mini loop bandA small continuous loopLeg and hip exercises around the thighs or ankles
Fabric loop bandA wider, cloth-covered loopMore comfortable on the skin; less likely to roll

Bands are usually colour-coded by strength, but colours vary between brands, so check the packaging. Start with the lightest or second-lightest band. If you have a latex allergy, choose latex-free bands. A set of three strengths lets you progress without buying more.

Grips and anchors for sore hands

Gripping a thin band tightly can strain painful fingers and thumbs. Try these instead:

  • Wrap, do not grip: lay the band across your palm and wrap it once around the back of your hand, so your hand holds it with an open palm.
  • Make a loop: tie a loop in each end and slip your hand or forearm through it.
  • Use handles: tube bands with padded handles, or add foam handles to a flat band.
  • Use your feet or a door anchor: stand or sit on the band, or use a door anchor (a strap that shuts in the door) at the right height, so your hands do less work.
  • Cuff straps: ankle or wrist cuffs that clip to a band avoid gripping altogether.

For hand-specific exercises, see our hand exercises for arthritis.

Safety checks before every session

  • Check the band for nicks, tears or sticky patches; replace it if damaged, as it can snap.
  • Make sure anchors are secure. Close the door fully on a door anchor and shut it on the hinge side, so it cannot open towards you.
  • Keep the band away from your face and eyes.
  • Warm up for 5 minutes, for example marching on the spot and arm circles.
  • Move slowly: about 2 seconds to stretch the band and 3 seconds to return. Control the return, do not let it snap back.
  • Breathe out as you stretch, in as you return. Do not hold your breath.
  • Use the 24-hour rule: mild aching that settles by the next day is fine; joint pain that lasts longer or swelling means do less next time.

Routine A: seated lower body (about 12 minutes)

Sit tall on a sturdy chair without wheels, feet flat. Do 8 to 12 repetitions of each, 1 to 2 sets.

  1. Seated leg press: loop the band around one foot and hold the ends at your hips. Bend the knee towards your chest, then push the foot forward to straighten the leg against the band. Return slowly.
  2. Seated knee extension: tie the band in a loop around the chair leg and your ankle. Straighten your knee against the band, hold for 2 seconds and lower.
  3. Seated hip abduction: place a loop band just above your knees. Push your knees apart against the band, then bring them back slowly.
  4. Ankle push: straighten one leg, loop the band around the ball of the foot and hold the ends. Point your foot down against the band, then return slowly.
  5. Seated march: loop a band around both thighs. Lift one knee a few centimetres, then the other.

Routine B: standing lower body (about 12 minutes)

Hold a worktop or sturdy chair for balance. Do 8 to 12 repetitions of each, 1 to 3 sets.

  1. Banded sit-to-stand: place a loop band just above your knees and do sit-to-stands from a chair, keeping your knees pressed gently out against the band.
  2. Side step: with a loop band around your ankles or above your knees, take small steps sideways along the worktop, then back.
  3. Standing hip extension: loop a band around both ankles. Keeping your body upright, take one leg slightly backwards against the band, then return.
  4. Standing hip abduction: with the band around your ankles, lift one leg out to the side, then return slowly.
  5. Mini squat with band: stand on the middle of a flat band holding the ends at shoulder height, and do a small, comfortable squat.

For more knee-specific exercises, see our knee exercises for osteoarthritis.

Routine C: upper body (about 12 minutes)

Seated or standing. Do 8 to 12 repetitions of each, 1 to 3 sets.

  1. Seated row: sit with legs straight or knees bent, loop the band around your feet and hold the ends. Pull your elbows back, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then return slowly.
  2. Chest press: wrap the band around your upper back, under your arms, holding the ends at chest level. Push your hands forward until your arms are nearly straight, then return.
  3. Pull-apart: hold the band in front of your chest with hands shoulder-width apart. Pull your hands outwards, squeezing your shoulder blades, then return.
  4. Outward rotation: elbows bent at your sides, hold the band between your hands. Keeping your elbows in, rotate your forearms outwards, then return.
  5. Bicep curl: stand or sit on the middle of the band, holding the ends with palms forward. Bend your elbows to bring your hands towards your shoulders, then lower slowly.
  6. Overhead press (if comfortable): sit on the band, holding the ends at shoulder height, and press up to just below straight. Keep it below shoulder height or skip it if your shoulders are painful.

Shoulder arthritis needs extra care with pressing and lifting; see our shoulder arthritis exercises.

A sample 20-minute full-body session

  1. Warm-up, 4 minutes: marching on the spot or seated marching, shoulder rolls, arm circles, ankle circles.
  2. Legs, 7 minutes: banded sit-to-stand, side steps (or seated hip abduction), seated knee extension.
  3. Upper body, 7 minutes: seated row, chest press, pull-apart, outward rotation.
  4. Cool-down, 2 minutes: slow walking or marching, then gentle stretches for the chest, calves and thighs.

Do 1 set of 10 for each exercise in the first weeks, resting 30 to 60 seconds between exercises. Later, do two rounds.

Track your progress

Keep a simple note of the band colour, sets and repetitions for each exercise, and how your joints felt the next day. Every 4 weeks, check something practical, such as how many sit-to-stands you can do in 30 seconds or how easily you can lift a shopping bag. Most people notice exercises feel easier within a few weeks, with clearer strength gains after 8 to 12 weeks.

Caring for your bands

Store bands out of direct sunlight and away from radiators, which can make the material brittle. Keep them away from sharp objects, jewellery and long fingernails. Wipe them clean with a damp cloth and let them dry. Replace bands that are thinning, sticky, cracked or have lost their stretch.

Putting it together: weekly options

Your situationSuggested plan
New to exercise or find standing hardRoutine A + Routine C (seated), 2 days a week
Can stand comfortably with supportRoutine B + Routine C, 2–3 days a week
Short on timePick 2 leg and 2 upper-body exercises, 10 minutes, 3 days a week
Flare daySkip band work on flaring joints; gentle movement only

A 10-week plan

WeeksSessionsSets and repsBand
1–22 a week1 set of 8–10Lightest, or no band to learn the movement
3–42 a week1–2 sets of 10–12Lightest
5–72–3 a week2 sets of 10–12Move up for exercises that feel easy
8–102–3 a week2–3 sets of 8–12Next strength up where ready

How to progress

Progress when you can do 12 slow, controlled repetitions with good form and your joints settle by the next day, for two sessions in a row. Change one thing at a time:

  1. add repetitions or a set
  2. shorten the band (hold it closer to the anchor) or step further away
  3. double the band or use the next strength
  4. slow the return to 4 seconds

If a joint flares, go back a step for a week. Bands lose some stretch over time; replace them if they no longer feel as firm.

Common mistakes

  • Using a band that is too strong and losing control of the movement.
  • Letting the band snap back instead of returning slowly.
  • Gripping too hard with painful hands; use loops, wraps or handles.
  • Shrugging the shoulders during upper-body exercises; keep them low and relaxed.
  • Locking the knees or elbows at the end of a movement.
  • Using worn or damaged bands.

Adapting for different conditions

  • Osteoarthritis of the knee or hip: focus on Routines A and B for the thigh and buttock muscles, keeping squats shallow.
  • Rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis: use lighter bands and loops rather than grips; reduce band work on inflamed joints during a flare.
  • After joint replacement: follow your physiotherapist's programme; bands are often used in rehabilitation but timing and positions matter.
  • Frailty or low strength: start with seated work; our guide to seated resistance bands for frail adults has gentler options.

When to get medical help

Stop the exercise if you get sharp pain, a joint locking or giving way, sudden swelling, or pins and needles or numbness.

  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or feeling faint that does not settle with rest.
  • Get urgent help if a band snaps and injures your eye; go to A&E or an eye casualty department, or call NHS 111.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature.
  • See your GP or a physiotherapist if exercise keeps making joint pain worse for more than a day, you are unsure which exercises suit you, or you are not getting stronger after 8 to 12 weeks. In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy.

Are resistance bands good for arthritis?

Yes. Bands provide smooth, adjustable resistance that is gentle on joints and lets you strengthen the muscles that support them. They are cheap, portable and can be used seated or standing.

Which resistance band strength should I start with?

Start with the lightest or second-lightest band. You should be able to do 8 to 12 slow repetitions with good form, finishing with the last few feeling hard. Colours vary by brand, so check the strength on the packaging.

How often should I use resistance bands?

Two or three times a week on non-consecutive days is enough to build strength. This meets the UK recommendation for muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days a week.

Can I use resistance bands with arthritis in my hands?

Yes, with the right grip. Wrap the band around an open hand, use loops or padded handles, or anchor the band under your feet or in a door so your hands do less work.

Are resistance bands as good as weights?

For most people with arthritis, bands can build useful strength just as well as light weights, especially at the start. Some people later add weights or gym machines for variety and heavier loads.

Can resistance bands snap?

They can, especially when worn or damaged. Check bands before each use, replace them when they show wear, keep them away from your face, and anchor them securely.
